domain: 장문맥 멀티턴 에이전트 서비스 (단일 세션 문맥이 100K 토큰을 넘고 대화가 이어지며 KV cache가 턴마다 누적되는 워크로드)
contrast_domains: 온디바이스 추론 (스마트폰과 엣지, 전력과 메모리 제약)
클라우드 대규모 동시 서빙 (수천 세션 동시 처리, 비용 민감)

MLA.approach: Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) reduces the heavy Key-Value (KV) cache bottleneck in inference by jointly compressing keys and values into a low-rank latent vector, achieving better performance than Multi-Head Attention (MHA) with significantly smaller KV cache requirements.
reported_numbers: 93.3% reduction in KV cache (compared to DeepSeek 67B)
5.76 times boost in maximum generation throughput (compared to DeepSeek 67B)
42.5% savings in training costs (compared to DeepSeek 67B)
MLA.scope: MLA operates within the Transformer framework and requires the model to support multi-head attention mechanisms with the ability to perform low-rank key-value joint compression. It is designed for large MoE language models supporting long context lengths (e.g., 128K).

ITME.approach: ITME addresses the large KV cache memory footprint by tiering LLM data types and offloading voluminous, predictable data such as model weights and long-context KV caches to a remote expansion tier using CXL-hybrid memory. It uses coordinated hardware/software prefetching to mask access latencies and hide storage and network overheads. This enables efficient multi-tier memory management compatible with existing software-level policies.
reported_numbers: up to a 35.7% throughput improvement over the CPU-offload baseline in extended turns (compared to CPU-offload baseline with 128 GB host memory) [ITME p.10]
128 GB host memory allocated for caching in CPU-offload baseline (benchmark setup) [ITME p.9]
CXL-hybrid memory tier labeled as T3.5, host memory as T2, with ITME using only a fraction of T2 as staging buffer [ITME p.9]
ITME.scope: Requires a multi-tier memory hierarchy including high-speed GPU or host memory tiers for activations and working KV cache, and a remote expansion tier with CXL-hybrid memory for large, predictable data types like weights and long-context KV caches. Relies on hardware-level prefetching from NVMe SSDs into DRAM cache within the CXL-hybrid memory and PCIe Gen5 interface for high bandwidth. Compatible with existing software-level multi-tier cache management policies.
ITME.limits: Performance fluctuations due to unpredictable I/O stalls during intense contention in the CXL-hybrid memory tier, though mitigated by read-priority scheduling. PCIe Gen4-based architectures in other systems limit bandwidth, but ITME uses PCIe Gen5 to address this. No other explicit limitations stated.

criterion_scores.채택_폭: DeepSeek-V2 MLA는 vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM 등 주요 추론 스택의 캐시 관리 인터페이스와 통합되어 있으며, SGLang에서는 FlashInfer의 MLA 전용 커널을 통해 처리된다. 그러나 MLA는 범용 추론 프레임워크에서 아직 지원되지 않아 DeepSeek-V3는 MHA와 동등한 메모리 크기를 사용해야 한다는 제약이 있다.[웹: Predictive Multi-Tier Memory Management for KV Cache in Large ...][웹: LLM Inference Kernels for vLLM and SGLang (2026 Guide)]
criterion_scores.채택_깊이: SGLang에서는 MLA가 기본값으로 사용되며, FlashInfer 기반 MLA 백엔드(FA3)가 명시적 백엔드 지정이 없을 때 기본으로 작동한다. MLA는 DeepSeek V2, V3, GLM-4.7-Flash 모델에서 자동으로 활성화된다.[웹: LLM Inference Kernels for vLLM and SGLang (2026 Guide)][웹: MLA (Multi-head Latent Attention) - mistral.rs Documentation]
criterion_scores.진입_비용: 기존 MHA 기반 LLM을 MLA로 전환하기 위해서는 MHA2MLA라는 파라미터 효율적 미세조정 프레임워크를 사용하며, 이는 전체 학습 데이터의 0.3%~0.6%만으로 재학습 없이 적응 가능하다. 즉, 완전한 재학습 없이도 기존 가중치를 최대한 재사용할 수 있으나, 완전한 zero-shot 전환은 불가능하다.[웹: Enabling DeepSeek's Multi-Head Latent Attention in Any ...]
criterion_scores.생태계_지지: MLA는 DeepSeek V2, V3, GLM-4.7-Flash 등 여러 모델에 적용되며, FlashInfer 라이브러리 등에서 지원되어 일부 추론 스택에 통합되어 있다. 그러나 독립된 제3자의 재현 결과나 표준 규격, 컨소시엄에 대한 언급은 없다.[웹: MLA (Multi-head Latent Attention) - mistral.rs Documentation][웹: LLM Inference Kernels for vLLM and SGLang (2026 Guide)][웹: Predictive Multi-Tier Memory Management for KV Cache in Large ...]
criterion_scores.시장_수치: LLM 비용 최적화 시장은 2025년 8억 6,370만 달러에서 2035년 92억 720만 달러로 연평균 26.7% 성장할 것으로 전망되며, 북미가 44.1% 점유율을 차지한다. 다만 이 수치는 LLM 비용 최적화 상위 범주를 가리키며, MLA 기술 자체에 대한 직접적 시장 규모나 성장 전망 수치는 없다.[웹: LLM Cost Optimization Market Size | CAGR of 26%]

pro: MLA는 vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM 등 주요 추론 스택의 캐시 관리 계층에 통합되어 있어 실서비스 적용 가능성이 높다.[웹: Predictive Multi-Tier Memory Management for KV Cache in Large ...]
SGLang에서는 MLA가 기본값으로 설정되어 있어 채택 깊이가 높다.[웹: LLM Inference Kernels for vLLM and SGLang (2026 Guide)]
기존 MHA 기반 모델을 적은 데이터로 미세조정하여 MLA로 전환할 수 있어 도입 비용이 낮다.[웹: Enabling DeepSeek's Multi-Head Latent Attention in Any ...]
MLA는 DeepSeek V2, V3, GLM-4.7-Flash 등 여러 모델에 적용되어 생태계 내에서 활용되고 있다.[웹: MLA (Multi-head Latent Attention) - mistral.rs Documentation]
con: MLA는 범용 추론 프레임워크에서 아직 지원되지 않아 일부 모델은 MHA와 동등한 메모리 크기를 사용해야 하는 제약이 있다.[웹: Predictive Multi-Tier Memory Management for KV Cache in Large ...]
독립된 제3자의 재현 결과나 표준 규격, 컨소시엄에 대한 정보가 없어 생태계 지지 측면에서 한계가 있다.[웹: LLM Inference Kernels for vLLM and SGLang (2026 Guide)]
시장 수치가 MLA 기술 자체가 아닌 상위 범주인 LLM 비용 최적화 시장을 가리키고 있어, MLA의 직접적 시장성 수치는 확인되지 않는다.[웹: LLM Cost Optimization Market Size | CAGR of 26%]
unknown: 시장_수치: MLA 기술 자체의 직접적인 시장 규모나 성장 전망 수치는 근거에 없다.

criterion_scores.채택_폭: ITME는 기존의 여러 소프트웨어 수준의 멀티티어 메모리 정책과 호환되며, ITME 자체가 고성능 공유 저장소 계층을 제공하는 아키텍처로 제안되었다. 그러나 ITME가 주요 추론 스택이나 상용 제품의 어느 계층(커널, 서빙 엔진, SDK, 하드웨어 제품)에 구현되었는지에 대한 직접적 언급은 없다[ITME p.11]. 웹 근거에서는 vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, SGLang 등이 계층화된 KV 저장소 계층을 지원한다고 하나, 이는 범주 수준의 관찰로 ITME 고유 근거로 사용하지 않았다.
criterion_scores.채택_깊이: ITME 문서에는 구현이 기본값인지 선택 옵션인지, 안정성 등급에 대한 정보가 없다. 웹 근거에서 주요 추론 프레임워크들이 KV 캐시 오프로딩을 기본 내장 기능으로 지원한다고 하나, 이는 범주 수준의 관찰로 ITME 고유 근거로 사용하지 않았다.
criterion_scores.진입_비용: ITME는 CXL 하이브리드 메모리를 활용하여 TB 단위의 메모리 확장을 제공하며, PCIe Gen5 인터페이스를 채택해 높은 대역폭을 지원한다. 기존 가중치나 재학습 필요성에 대한 언급은 없으며, 새 하드웨어(CXL 하이브리드 메모리) 도입이 필요함을 시사한다[ITME p.11].
criterion_scores.생태계_지지: ITME는 CXL 기반 메모리 확장 연구의 연장선상에 있으며, CXL 기술은 컨소시엄이 존재하고 여러 연구가 진행 중이다. 그러나 ITME 자체를 베이스라인으로 한 후속 연구, 독립 제3자 재현 결과, 표준 규격 내역은 문서에 없다[ITME p.11].
criterion_scores.시장_수치: CXL 메모리 확장 시장은 2025년 13억 달러 규모이며, 2026-2034년 연평균 성장률 28.7%로 2034년 118억 달러에 이를 것으로 전망된다. AI 및 머신러닝 추론이 주요 응용 분야로 38.5% 매출 점유율을 차지한다. 다만 이 수치는 ITME가 아닌 CXL 메모리 확장 범주에 대한 시장 전망이다[웹: CXL Memory Expansion Market Research Report 2034].

pro: ITME는 기존 멀티티어 메모리 정책과 호환되며 고성능 공유 저장소 계층을 제공하는 아키텍처로 설계되었다[ITME p.11].
ITME는 PCIe Gen5 인터페이스를 채택한 CXL 하이브리드 메모리를 활용해 높은 대역폭을 제공한다[ITME p.11].
CXL 메모리 확장 시장은 AI 추론을 포함한 분야에서 빠르게 성장 중이며, 2025년 13억 달러에서 2034년 118억 달러로 확대될 전망이다[웹: CXL Memory Expansion Market Research Report 2034].
con: ITME가 주요 추론 스택이나 상용 제품의 어느 계층에 구현되었는지에 대한 직접적 근거가 없다[ITME p.11].
ITME 구현의 안정성 등급, 기본값 여부 등 채택 깊이에 관한 정보가 없다[ITME p.11].
ITME 자체를 베이스라인으로 한 후속 연구, 독립 제3자 재현 결과, 표준 규격 관련 근거가 없다[ITME p.11].
시장 수치는 ITME가 아닌 CXL 메모리 확장 범주에 대한 것이며, ITME 고유 시장성 수치는 없다[웹: CXL Memory Expansion Market Research Report 2034].
unknown: 채택_폭: ITME가 주요 추론 스택 및 상용 제품의 어느 계층에 구현되었는지 구체적 근거 없음.
채택_깊이: ITME 구현이 기본값인지 선택 옵션인지, 안정성 등급에 관한 정보 없음.
진입_비용: ITME 도입 시 기존 가중치 재사용 여부, 재학습 필요성에 관한 정보 없음.
생태계_지지: ITME를 베이스라인으로 한 후속 연구, 독립 제3자 재현 결과, 표준 규격 존재 여부에 관한 정보 없음.
시장_수치: ITME 고유 시장 규모나 성장 전망 수치 없음.

criterion_scores.병목_일치: 장문맥 멀티턴 에이전트 서비스에서 메모리 용량과 대역폭이 지배적인 병목이며, MLA는 KV 캐시를 크게 줄여 메모리 및 대역폭 병목을 완화한다. 특히 128K 토큰 문맥에서 MLA는 약 8GB KV 캐시를 요구해 MHA(512GB) 대비 현저히 적은 메모리를 사용한다.[MLA p.6][웹: DualPath: Breaking the Storage Bandwidth Bottleneck in Agentic LLM Inference][웹: Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) on GPU Cloud: Cut KV Cache][웹: Understanding DeepSeek's Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) | Shashank Shekhar]
criterion_scores.자원_전제: 이 도메인에서 요구하는 대규모 GPU 메모리(수백 GB 이상)와 KV 캐시 메모리 요구를 MLA가 줄여 다중 사용자 동시 처리에 유리하다. 다만 DeepSeek 모델 자체가 매우 크고, 최신 GPU와 멀티노드 인프라가 필요하다.[웹: The complete DeepSeek model guide | Guides][웹: Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) on GPU Cloud: Cut KV Cache][웹: Understanding DeepSeek's Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) | Shashank Shekhar]
criterion_scores.정확도_허용치: MLA는 MHA 대비 성능 저하 없이 또는 더 나은 성능을 보이며, 87.5% KV 캐시 압축 시 약 3% 정확도 손실(모델 크기 Llama2-7B, 문맥 길이 장문맥, 과제 종류는 일반적 LLM 평가)로 보고되었다. 4비트 양자화와 결합 시 최대 3.2% 손실까지 허용 가능하다.[MLA p.6][웹: Enabling DeepSeek's Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) on GPU Cloud: Cut KV Cache]
criterion_scores.운영_비용: MLA 도입 시 KV 캐시 압축과 쿼리 흡수(Absorption) 등 추가 연산이 필요하나, 별도의 패치 관리나 신규 인프라 도입 없이 기존 GPU 클라우드 환경에서 운영 가능하다. 다만 압축된 KV 캐시를 처리하는 특수 커널(FlashInfer MLA kernel) 사용으로 운영 복잡도가 다소 증가할 수 있다.[웹: Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) on GPU Cloud: Cut KV Cache][웹: Understanding DeepSeek's Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) | Shashank Shekhar]
criterion_scores.증거_성숙도: MLA는 DeepSeek V2 모델에 실제 적용되어 128K 토큰 문맥에서 KV 캐시 크기와 성능을 측정한 저자 자체 보고이며, 일부 제3자(예: Moonshot AI Kimi K2 시리즈)도 관련 아키텍처를 사용한다. 다만 독립적 제3자 검증은 제한적이다.[MLA p.6][웹: Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) on GPU Cloud: Cut KV Cache][웹: The complete DeepSeek model guide | Guides]

pro: MLA는 KV 캐시를 MHA 대비 최대 64배까지 줄여 장문맥 멀티턴 에이전트 서비스의 메모리 및 대역폭 병목을 효과적으로 완화한다.[MLA p.6][웹: Understanding DeepSeek's Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) | Shashank Shekhar]
MLA는 MHA 대비 성능 저하 없이 KV 캐시를 크게 압축하며, 87.5% 압축 시 약 3% 정확도 손실로 장문맥 LLM 과제에 적합하다.[웹: Enabling DeepSeek's Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) on GPU Cloud: Cut KV Cache]
MLA는 기존 GPU 클라우드 인프라에서 추가 인프라 없이 운영 가능하며, 압축된 KV 캐시를 처리하는 특수 커널로 디코딩 속도도 20-35% 개선된다.[웹: Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) on GPU Cloud: Cut KV Cache]
con: DeepSeek 모델 자체가 매우 크고, 최신 GPU 및 멀티노드 인프라가 필요해 인프라 요구가 높으며, KV 캐시 압축에도 불구하고 대규모 메모리 요구는 여전하다.[웹: The complete DeepSeek model guide | Guides]
MLA 도입 시 쿼리 흡수 및 압축 해제 연산이 추가되어 운영 복잡도가 증가할 수 있으며, 별도의 패치 관리나 신규 전송 계층 도입은 없으나 특수 커널 사용이 필요하다.[웹: Understanding DeepSeek's Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) | Shashank Shekhar]
MLA의 성능 및 효율성 평가는 주로 저자 자체 보고에 의존하며, 독립적 제3자 검증은 제한적이다.[MLA p.6][웹: Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) on GPU Cloud: Cut KV Cache]
unknown: 정확도_허용치: 구체적 장문맥 멀티턴 에이전트 서비스 특화 과제에서의 정확도 손실 범위 및 측정 조건 상세 정보는 근거에 명확히 제시되어 있지 않음.
운영_비용: 별도 패치 관리, 신규 인프라, 전송 계층 추가 등 구체적 운영 비용 변화에 대한 정량적 데이터는 근거에 없음.

criterion_scores.병목_일치: 이 도메인에서 메모리 용량과 대역폭이 주요 병목이며, ITME는 대용량 모델 가중치와 장문맥 KV 캐시를 CXL 하이브리드 메모리 원격 확장 계층에 오프로드하여 용량 병목을 해결하고, 하드웨어/소프트웨어 선행 로딩으로 지연과 네트워크 오버헤드를 숨긴다. 다만 대역폭 병목에 대한 직접적 언급은 없으며, 대역폭 중요성은 범주 근거에서 확인된다.[ITME p.2][웹: AdaptiveKV: Accelerating KV Cache Offloading with a ...]
criterion_scores.자원_전제: ITME는 PCIe Gen5 인터페이스를 사용하는 CXL 하이브리드 메모리 아키텍처를 전제로 하며, 이는 상용 CXL 하드웨어가 제한적인 상황에서 FPGA 프로토타입으로 구현되었다. 따라서 실제 도메인에서 PCIe Gen5 및 CXL 하이브리드 메모리 사용이 전제되어야 한다.[ITME p.11]
criterion_scores.운영_비용: ITME는 사용자 수준 선행 로딩 API를 제공하여 LLM 추론 프레임워크가 데이터 전송을 제어할 수 있으나, 별도 패치 관리나 신규 인프라 도입, 전송 계층 추가에 대한 구체적 언급은 없다.[ITME p.2]
criterion_scores.증거_성숙도: ITME는 Llama-3.1 8B 및 70B 모델과 ShareGPT, Mooncake 데이터셋을 사용해 다중 턴 대화 워크로드에서 성능을 평가했으며, FPGA 기반 프로토타입과 생산급 SK hynix CMM을 활용해 자체 측정한 결과를 보고한다. 제3자 검증 근거는 없다.[ITME p.9][ITME p.11]

pro: ITME는 장문맥 KV 캐시와 모델 가중치의 예측 가능성과 대용량 특성을 활용해 원격 확장 계층에 오프로드하고, 하드웨어/소프트웨어 선행 로딩으로 지연과 네트워크 오버헤드를 효과적으로 숨긴다.[ITME p.2]

con: 도메인에서 KV 캐시 오프로드 시 DDR 대역폭 병목이 중요하나, ITME 근거에서는 대역폭 병목 해소에 대한 구체적 수치나 전략이 부족하다.[웹: AdaptiveKV: Accelerating KV Cache Offloading with a ...]

evidence.full: 2.1. Multi-Head Latent Attention: Boosting Inference Efficiency Conventional Transformer models usually adopts Multi-Head Attention (MHA) (Vaswani et al., 2017), but during generation, its heavy Key-Value (KV) cache will become the bottleneck that limit the inference efficiency. In order to reduce the KV cache, Multi-Query Attention (MQA) (Shazeer, 2019) and Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) (Ainslie et al., 2023) are proposed. They require a smaller magnitude of KV cache, but their performance does not match MHA (we provide the ablation of MHA, GQA and MQA in Appendix D.1). For DeepSeek-V2, we design an innovative attention mechanism called Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA). Equipped with low-rank key-value joint compression, MLA achieves better performance than MHA, but requires a significantly smaller amount of KV cache. We introduce its architecture in the following, and also provide a comparison between MLA and MHA in Appendix D.2. 2.1.1. Preliminaries: Standard Multi-Head Attention

evidence.full: 5. Conclusion, Limitation, and Future Work In this paper, we introduce DeepSeek-V2, a large MoE language model that supports 128K context length. In addition to strong performance, it is also characterized by economical training and efficient inference, benefiting from its innovative architecture including MLA and DeepSeekMoE. In practice, compared with DeepSeek 67B, DeepSeek-V2 achieves significantly stronger performance, and meanwhile saves 42.5% of training costs, reduces the KV cache by 93.3%, and boosts the maximum generation throughput to 5.76 times. Evaluation results further demonstrate that with only 21B activated parameters, DeepSeek-V2 achieves top-tier performance among open-source models and becomes the strongest open-source MoE model.

By default, vLLM handles host memory pressure by evicting and recomputing KV caches, which incurs significant overhead. To create a competitive and realistic baseline, we developed vLLM, an extended version of vLLM with the following custom implementations: • NVMe-oF Integration: We integrated an NVMe-oF (NVMe over Fabrics) stack to enable storage access. DeepSeek models use this to reduce KV cache memory by 60-70% compared to standard MHA. When using `--attention-backend flashinfer`, SGLang routes MLA computation through FlashInfer's dedicated MLA kernel, which handles the compressed format directly and reduces attention compute time by 20-35% compared to the decomposed expansion-then-attention path. For DeepSeek-V2, we design an innovative attention mechanism called Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA). Equipped with low-rank key-value joint compression, MLA achieves better performance than MHA, but requires a significantly smaller amount of KV cache. We introduce its architecture in the following, and also provide a comparison between MLA and MHA in Appendix D.2. 2.1.1. Preliminaries: Standard Multi-Head Attention

Press `Esc` to hide this help. # mistral.rs Documentation. # Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) in mistral.rs. Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) is an efficient attention mechanism that reduces KV cache memory usage by compressing key-value states into a low-rank latent space. This technique was introduced in DeepSeek V2 and is also used in DeepSeek V3 and GLM-4.7-Flash models. MLA compresses the key-value cache by:. 1. Projecting KV states into a compact latent representation (`kv_lora_rank` dimensions). 2. Storing only the compressed latent vectors and rotary position embeddings in the KV cache. 3. Reconstructing full KV states on-the-fly during attention computation. This results in significant memory savings compared to standard multi-head attention, enabling longer context lengths with the same GPU memory. MLA is automatically enabled for the following model architectures when using PagedAttention on CUDA:. | DeepSeek V2 | `deepseekv2` | kv\_lora\_rank varies |. | DeepSeek V3 | `deepseekv3` | kv\_lora\_rank=512, kpe\_head\_dim=64 |. | GLM-4.7-Flash | `glm4moelite` | kv\_lora\_rank=512, kpe\_head\_dim=64 |. When these conditions are met, MLA is automatically used during the decode phase for optimal performance. 1. **Reduced KV Cache Memory**: The compressed latent representation uses significantly less memory than full key-value states, allowing for:. 2. **Optimized Decode Kernels**: Custom FlashInfer-based MLA kernels accelerate single-token generation by:. * Operating directly on compressed latent states. If you encounter issues or want to compare performance, you can disable MLA by setting the environment variable:. When disabled, the model falls back to standard PagedAttention with full KV cache storage. ### KV Cache Layout. When MLA is enabled, PagedAttention uses a specialized cache layout:. * **Key cache**: Stores compressed latent vectors (`kv_lora_rank` dimensions) + rotary position embeddings (`kpe_head_dim` dimensions). * **Value cache**: Shares the same block structure for efficient memory management. ### Decode Path. During single-token generation (decode phase):. 1. Query is projected to latent space. 2. Attention is computed directly on compressed KV states using FlashInfer MLA kernels. 1. Full KV states are computed for the current chunk. 2. Compressed latents are stored in the PagedAttention cache. * GLM-4.7-Flash - Model documentation.

[...] As downstream tasks grow increasingly com-plex, long-context processing and computationally intensive inference have become central to LLM ap-plications (An et al., 2024). A key bottleneck lies in the memory footprint of the Key-Value (KV) cache inherent to the Multi-Head Attention (MHA, 2017) mechanism, which scales linearly with sequence length and model size. To mitigate this, variants like Grouped-Query Attention (GQA, 2023) and Multi-Query Attention (MQA, 2019) have been ex-plored. However, these methods reduce not only the KV cache size but also the number of parame-ters in the attention, leading to performance degra-dation. The DeepSeek introduces Multi-Head La-tent Attention (MLA, 2024), an attention mecha-nism equipped with low-rank key-value joint com-pression. Empirically, MLA [...] • we demonstrate that the MHA2MLA architecture can be integrated with KV-cache quantization to achieve more economical inference (up to a 96.87% reduction). • we conduct experiments across five model sizes (from 135M to 13B, covering both MHA and GQA), and detailed ablation studies to provide guidance and insights for MHA2MLA.

evidence.full: A critical yet unexplored question arises: Can LLMs originally well-trained for MHA be adapted to enabling MLA for inference? The inherent architectural disparities between MHA and MLA render zero-shot transfer impractical, while the prohibitive cost of pretraining from scratch makes this transition both technically challenging and underexplored in existing research. To address this gap, we propose the first carefully designed MHA2MLA framework that maximizes parameter reuse from pre-trained MHA networks while aligning the KV cache storage and inference process with MLA’s paradigm (Figure 1). Our framework features two pivotal technical innovations: partial rotary position embedding (partial RoPE) and low-rank approximation. [...] Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) is an innovative architecture proposed by DeepSeek, designed to ensure efficient and economical inference by significantly compressing the Key-Value (KV) cache into a latent vector. Compared to MLA, standard LLMs employing Multi-Head Attention (MHA) and its variants such as Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) exhibit significant cost disadvantages. Enabling well-trained LLMs (e.g., Llama) to rapidly adapt to MLA without pre-training from scratch is both meaningful and challenging. This paper proposes the first data-efficient fine-tuning method for transitioning from MHA to MLA (MHA2MLA), which includes two key components: for partial-RoPE, we remove RoPE from dimensions of queries and keys that contribute less to the attention scores, [...] MLA reduces memory footprint by projecting keys and values into a low-rank latent representation space (stored in the KV cache). MHA2MLA can also apply low-rank approximation to the values and keys stripped of RoPE (NoPE dimensions). By performing Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) on the pre-trained parameter matrices 𝑾v\bm{W}\_{v} and 𝑾k\bm{W}\_{k} corresponding to the NoPE subspaces, we compress these components into a latent space while maximizing the retention of knowledge learned by the original model. Our main contributions are: we introduce MHA2MLA, the first parameter-efficient fine-tuning framework that adapts pre-trained MHA-based LLMs to the MLA architecture using only 3‰ to 6‰ of training data without training from scratch.

This is the very real, very painful "memory wall" that has plagued LLMs, despite their computational prowess. It's not about the speed of computation anymore; it's about the speed and quantity of data that can be _stored and accessed_ during inference. evidence.full: ### 05 Does MLA help with throughput or just memory? Both. The primary gain is memory: smaller KV cache means more concurrent users per GPU, which directly multiplies throughput for multi-user workloads. A secondary gain comes from reduced HBM bandwidth pressure during decode - loading a 1,024-byte latent vector per layer is 64x less HBM traffic than loading full MHA KV pairs. For long-context workloads (32K+), memory bandwidth is often the bottleneck in decode, so MLA's smaller working set reduces both memory pressure and attention compute time. The FlashInfer MLA kernel in SGLang reduces attention compute time a further 20-35% on top by handling the compressed format natively. Back to all posts ## Related Reading More on Kernel Development → [...] The formula for KV cache memory per attention layer: MHA: `2 × num_heads × head_dim × 2 bytes × num_tokens` GQA (8 groups): `2 × num_groups × head_dim × 2 bytes × num_tokens` MLA: `d_c × 2 bytes × num_tokens` For DeepSeek V3 with 128 heads, head_dim=128, d_c=512, and 60 transformer layers: | Config | MHA (baseline) | GQA (8 groups, Llama 3 style) | MLA (DeepSeek V3) | --- --- | | KV bytes per token per layer | 65,536 | 4,096 | 1,024 | | KV cache at 128K ctx, 1 user, 60 layers | ~480 GB | ~30 GB | ~7.5 GB | | KV cache at 32K ctx, 1 user, 60 layers | ~120 GB | ~7.5 GB | ~1.9 GB | | Max concurrent users on H200 141 GB (after ~75 GB weights) | 0 | ~2 | ~8-9 | [...] vLLM defaults to absorbed MLA for DeepSeek models. SGLang with FlashInfer also defaults to absorbed for DeepSeek. For memory-bound deployments (long context, large batch), absorbed is the right choice: fewer memory reads per decode step beats the slightly higher static weight footprint. For compute-bound deployments where VRAM is the hard constraint (trying to fit a larger model), unabsorbed can recover 10-20% of VRAM at the cost of more FLOPs per token. When sizing GPU instances, check whether the benchmark figures for a model assumed absorbed or unabsorbed weights. evidence.full: Let's recall the problem: in standard Multi-Head Attention (MHA), the cache size per token is 2 × nh × dh (where nh is the number of heads and dh is the dimension per head). For a large model, this can be enormous. In MLA, we are no longer storing the full Key and Value vectors. We are only storing the tiny, shared latent vector, c_KV. The size of this vector is dc. The results from the DeepSeek team speak for themselves. Image 19 As shown in their research, compared to their powerful 67B dense model, DeepSeek-V2 with MLA reduces the KV cache size by an incredible 93.3%! [...] For every token in every sequence in every batch, we need to store _two_ vectors (Key and Value) for _each_ attention head in _each_ Transformer layer. So, the total KV Cache size per layer is roughly: 2 × L × d × nh (elements) And for the entire model, it's N_layers × (2 × L × d × nh). Consider DeepSeek-V2, for instance. It boasts a context length of 128,000 tokens. Imagine trying to hold a KV Cache for that many tokens! A single full-sized KV Cache for a large LLM can easily consume tens to hundreds of gigabytes of GPU memory. This immense memory footprint leads to critical limitations: [...] 3. High Inference Costs: More memory means more expensive GPUs, and lower throughput means more GPUs needed to serve the same number of users, driving up operational costs. This is the very real, very painful "memory wall" that has plagued LLMs, despite their computational prowess. It's not about the speed of computation anymore; it's about the speed and quantity of data that can be _stored and accessed_ during inference. Image 5 As you can see in that graph, DeepSeek-V2 dramatically reduces the KV Cache size(by 93.3%) compared to its predecessor, DeepSeek 67B. This isn't just a minor improvement; it's a monumental achievement that unlocks truly efficient large-scale LLM deployment.

In FP8, each billion parameters requires ~1 GB of VRAM to load. Plus, you’ll want to reserve a substantial amount of GPU memory for the KV cache (a few 100 GB extra). Even on the latest Blackwell-series GPUs (B200s), DeepSeek V3, R1, and V4 can’t fit on a single GPU. To run DeepSeek across a single GPU node (consisting of 8 GPUs), you’ll need to leverage model parallelism techniques, and depending on your hardware generation and precision, V4 Pro may require multi-node inference where V3 and R1 did not. [...] All of these optimizations are part of our LLM model runtime, and the performance benefits they bring carry over to other model families, including Kimi, Llama, and Qwen. ## Conclusion The DeepSeek models are powerful tools for AI applications, from chatbots and assistants to RAG pipelines and agents. That said, achieving the performance, reliability, and cost-efficiency necessary for consumer-facing applications requires a lot more than just an inference framework and some GPUs. DeepSeek’s massive size makes it challenging to deploy, scale, and optimize for production. To do so, you’ll need to leverage tools and techniques at the infrastructure and model runtime layers, like cross-cloud capacity management, tensor and expert parallelism, KV caching, and decoding techniques. evidence.full: What hardware does DeepSeek-V3 require for production inference? DeepSeek-V3 has 671 billion total parameters and requires approximately 700 GB of VRAM at FP8 precision for weight storage alone. The minimum practical production configuration is 8x H200 SXM GPUs (1,128 GB combined VRAM), which provides headroom for KV cache and activations alongside the model weights. An 8x H100 SXM configuration (640 GB total) can run the model at INT4 quantization with a 5 to 15 percent quality tradeoff on reasoning tasks. For production workloads requiring FP8 quality on H100 hardware, a 16-GPU configuration is needed. NVLink interconnects are important for this model's MoE routing communication patterns: SXM form factor with NVLink is strongly preferred over PCIe for multi-GPU DeepSeek-V3 deployments. [...] US government and defense workloads: The official DeepSeek API is not viable. Self-hosting on US-based infrastructure with FedRAMP-aligned providers is the only option. Healthcare workloads under HIPAA: Data routed through the official DeepSeek API cannot be HIPAA-compliant. US-hosted providers with BAA agreements (Fireworks AI is HIPAA-certified, GMI Cloud can discuss compliance requirements) are required. EU-hosted providers (Nebius, Scaleway) or US providers with adequate transfer mechanisms are required. Self-hosting on EU-based GPU infrastructure is the cleanest solution.

Multi-Head Latent Attention: Boosting Inference Efficiency Conventional Transformer models usually adopts Multi-Head Attention (MHA) (Vaswani et al., 2017), but during generation, its heavy Key-Value (KV) cache will become the bottleneck that limit the inference efficiency. In order to reduce the KV cache, Multi-Query Attention (MQA) (Shazeer, 2019) and Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) (Ainslie et al., 2023) are proposed. For DeepSeek-V2, we design an innovative attention mechanism called Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA). Equipped with low-rank key-value joint compression, MLA achieves better performance than MHA, but requires a significantly smaller amount of KV cache. (2024). evidence.full: Source: DeepSeek V3 The Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) was introduced with the release of the DeepSeek-V2 a variant of multi-head attention (MHA). It belongs to a family of techniques designed to address a key challenge in scaling large models: reducing the KV-cache size, which can become a major memory bottleneck. Other methods in this category include Group-Query Attention and Multi-Query Attention. While these approaches help lower memory usage, they often come with a tradeoff—sacrificing some performance in exchange for greater scalability. [...] Only the new query (Q) is computed. Previously cached key-value pairs (K, V) are reused. The attention mechanism then processes the new Q alongside the stored K and V. The latest tokens K and V are added to the cache for future steps. This approach reduces computational overhead, making autoregressive models more efficient. However, it comes with a trade-off: Increased memory usage. Since the KV cache scales proportionally with factors like batch size, sequence length, hidden size, and the number of attention heads, it can quickly become a memory bottleneck—especially for large batches or long sequences. ### Overcoming the Memory Challenge Source: DeepSeek V2 To tackle these memory constraints, two key strategies have emerged: [...] ### Standard Multi-Head Attention and Its Limitations Multi-head attention (MHA) enhances a model’s ability to capture diverse relationships in data by processing queries, keys, and values independently across multiple attention heads. However, this flexibility comes at a cost, especially during inference. The KV cache, which stores keys and values from previous tokens, expands linearly with sequence length. This quickly becomes a bottleneck, consuming significant GPU memory for long sequences. evidence.claim: When an artificial intelligence reads a 1,000-page legal contract to answer a single question, it commits a massive act of thermodynamic waste. To “remember” the book during the conversation, the AI must store mathematical representations of every single word in its short-term memory, known as the KV Cache. As the context length grows to 128,000 tokens or beyond, this cache balloons exponentially.
evidence.full: When an artificial intelligence reads a 1,000-page legal contract to answer a single question, it commits a massive act of thermodynamic waste. To “remember” the book during the conversation, the AI must store mathematical representations of every single word in its short-term memory, known as the KV Cache. As the context length grows to 128,000 tokens or beyond, this cache balloons exponentially. The AI does not run out of “thinking” power; it simply runs out of expensive High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM) on the server, triggering an Out of Memory (OOM) crash. This memory-bound bottleneck is why cloud providers charge exorbitant fees for long-context prompts, and why a single data center requires thousands of $30,000 NVIDIA GPUs just to handle basic user traffic. [...] ## Case Study Situation: By late 2024, the AI industry hit a scaling wall. Users demanded larger context windows to process entire codebases and books. However, serving a 128,000-token context using standard Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) required gigabytes of High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM) per user. Cloud providers were forced to limit context lengths, charge extreme premiums, or suffer horrific latency degradation during peak hours. Challenge: Engineer an attention mechanism that drastically reduced the memory footprint of the KV Cache to levels below MQA, without sacrificing the elite, state-of-the-art reasoning capabilities required for complex math and coding benchmarks. [...] During the “pre-fill” phase (when you paste a document into ChatGPT), the GPUs run at maximum compute capacity. But during the “decoding” phase (when the AI types its answer out word-by-word), the GPUs sit idle. They are starving for data. They have to fetch the massive KV Cache from memory for every single word generated. Moving gigabytes of data across the silicon chips is incredibly slow. By slashing the KV cache by 93%, MLA allows the entirety of a massive context window to fit directly into the ultra-fast SRAM (Static RAM) located right next to the processor cores, rather than the slower HBM. This eliminates the data-transfer traffic jam, allowing the AI to generate text at blistering speeds, multiplying the total number of users a single server can handle simultaneously.

evidence.full: DeepSeek shipped MLA in production twice: first in DeepSeek-V2 (236B total, 21B active), then at far larger scale in DeepSeek-V3 (671B total, 37B active), where MLA and the DeepSeekMoE sparse-expert architecture together are credited with keeping training cost down to roughly $5.576M in compute at assumed 2024 H800 rental prices, alongside efficient inference at deployment (DeepSeek-AI, 2024, arXiv:2412.19437). The technique has since spread beyond DeepSeek's own lab. Moonshot AI's Kimi K2, a 1-trillion-parameter, 32B-active MoE model, adopts MLA directly, citing the same rationale: KV cache footprint matters disproportionately for long-context and multi-agent serving workloads, where many concurrent sessions each hold a large context in memory simultaneously (Kimi Team, 2025, [...] > Why this matters: Every production LLM serving system is bottlenecked less by raw compute than by how many bytes it must move from GPU memory for every generated token. The key-value cache, not the model weights, is usually what limits how many users a single GPU can serve concurrently at long context lengths. MLA attacks that bottleneck directly, and its adoption by DeepSeek-V3, Kimi K2, and (in descendant form) GLM-5 has made it one of the most consequential architecture choices in open-weight LLMs since Grouped-Query Attention. ## TL;DR [...] Scale this out to a full request. For a 128K-token context, DeepSeek-V2's maximum supported length, and a 60-layer model, the MHA-style cache would need roughly \(65{,}536 \times 128{,}000 \times 60 \approx 503\) GB per sequence, which is far beyond what a single accelerator or even a small cluster could hold for one user, let alone a batch of concurrent users. The MLA-style cache for the same sequence needs roughly \(1{,}152 \times 128{,}000 \times 60 \approx 8.8\) GB, comfortably fitting alongside model weights on realistic serving hardware. That gap, not the exact percentage, is the entire economic argument for MLA at long context.

evidence.full: LMCache is a vendor-neutral KV cache management layer designed to optimize LLM inference by reducing TTFT and increasing throughput, especially for long-context workloads. It supports persistent, tiered KV cache offloading to various storage backends including CPU RAM, local disk, Redis, Valkey, Mooncake, and InfiniStore. Mooncake Store is a distributed KV cache storage engine designed specifically for LLM inference. It enables inference engines to store, retrieve, and transfer KV caches across GPUs, nodes, and instances, supporting prefill-decode disaggregation and improving cache reuse. It is widely integrated with systems such as vLLM, SGLang, and LMCache. [...] ## How to offload the KV cache​ You almost certainly don't need to build the implementation yourself. Every major inference framework now supports KV cache offloading as a built-in feature, and a second layer of dedicated KV cache systems exists for the cases the framework can't cover on its own. ### Built-in offloading in your inference framework​ vLLM, SGLang, and MAX all support offloading to host memory and disk with no extra infrastructure. The mechanism is similar: they extend the existing prefix cache so that completed blocks are demoted to a larger, slower tier, then promoted back to the GPU when a later request hits them. Transfers can run asynchronously on DMA (Direct Memory Access) copy engines, so they overlap with model execution rather than stalling it. [...] --kv-offloading-size 100 # the buffer size in GiB ``` Recent vLLM versions expose offloading through these two top-level flags. The underlying mechanism is the OffloadingConnector, which you can configure directly for multi-tier setups: ``` vllm serve --model meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct \ --kv-transfer-config '{ "kv_connector": "OffloadingConnector", "kv_role": "kv_both", "kv_connector_extra_config": { "cpu_bytes_to_use": 100000000000, "spec_name": "TieringOffloadingSpec", "secondary_tiers": [{"type": "fs", "root_dir": "/mnt/kv_cache"}] } }' ``` ``` sglang serve --model-path meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct \ --enable-hierarchical-cache \ --hicache-ratio 2 \ # Host memory ratio (2x GPU memory)

evidence.full: Storing KV cache in GPU memory for LLM inference can quickly lead to memory saturation, limiting serving scalability and performance. KV cache storage on CPU memory becomes limited as model size and request context length increase. To that extent, we explore CXL memory for KV cache offloading, in which CXL offers expanded capacity with low-latency access. Our preliminary results show that CXL-CPU data transfer has similar latency and bandwidth as the CPU-GPU counterpart. In addition, CXL-based KV cache offloading provides similar performance compared to full KV re-compute on GPUs, while supporting larger workloads. Specifically, using CXL memory for KV cache storage increased the maximum batch size by 30%, while maintaining the same SLO on TTFT. Our cost-efficiency analysis further shows [...] service-level objective (SLO) for TTFT is typically 400ms . To meet such SLO, LLM serving systems often cache the previously-computed KV data of the preceding tokens (i.e., prefix) in GPU memory, to avoid re-computing them for future requests that have the same prefix [5, 3, 6]. Storing KV cache reduces the overall computational load and significantly improves throughput by trading memory for computation. As context length and concurrency grow, KV cache exceeds GPU memory and must be spilled, refilled, prefetched, and reused across the memory hierarchy. This is especially challenging for edge AI servers with 4 to 8 GPUs, where host DRAM capacity, DRAM bandwidth, PCIe bandwidth, power, and cost are tightly constrained. This model is attractive for distributed LLM serving because reusable KV states can be shared across [...] Long-context, multi-turn, and agentic LLM workloads increasingly reuse previously processed context, making KV-cache reuse essential for reducing redundant computation. However, this reuse shifts the bottleneck to the memory tier that stores and serves reusable KV states at cluster scale. GPU HBM and host DRAM are too costly to scale to TB-scale shared context capacity, motivating remote tiers built from lower-cost, higher-capacity media. [...] HyMCache differs from these efforts in both target workload and system interface. Rather than using CXL memory as a generic memory expansion tier, HyMCache targets remote KV caching for multi-turn and agentic LLM serving. In this setting, KV accesses are large, read-heavy, and predictable because prefix KV blocks are repeatedly reused across turns. evidence.full: Title: KV Cache Offloading for LLM Inference Using CXL-UEC Fabrics (Part II) # KV Cache Offloading for LLM Inference Using CXL-UEC Fabrics (Part II). Recent industry momentum has begun converging CXL memory semantics with datacenter-scale fabrics, though each effort addresses only a fragment of the full problem. TraCT (December 2024) demonstrates CXL-attached shared memory for KV cache across multiple GPUs, enabling efficient cache sharing without network overhead. CXL-SpecKV explores FPGA-based speculative prefetch for KV cache, showing that hardware acceleration can reduce cache miss penalties. Yet it operates within CXL only, and its speculation strategy is position-based rather than attention-based, missing the opportunity to exploit the actual access patterns that transformer models exhibit. ### The Gap. The infrastructure for CXL-over-fabric is materializing. Enfabrica's architecture proves that the mechanical challenges of exposing CXL.mem load/store semantics across a UEC-class network are solvable. No architecture exploits the spatial locality inherent in RoPE positional encodings to prefetch intelligently. My work bridges that gap with a model-aware cache management architecture that sits atop emerging CXL-UEC infrastructure and makes tiering, eviction, and prefetch decisions based on learned access patterns from transformer attention—not generic LRU heuristics. I alos suggested we exploit RoPE locality through attention-aware spatial prefetch. Because rotary position embeddings create predictable attention patterns—approximately 75% of attention mass falls within ±128 positions of the query—we prefetch speculatively within this window, hiding the latency of CXL and UEC access behind computation. We then integrate with UEC congestion control, adapting prefetch aggressiveness based on network backpressure signals. When bandwidth is available, we prefetch aggressively from remote CXL pools. For systems audiences, this is the first attention-aware tiered memory architecture for LLM inference, exploiting CXL's load/store semantics locally and UEC's RDMA capabilities at datacenter scale. The contribution is architectural: a new point in the design space that couples memory management policy with model semantics. By using per-head EMA tracking to drive eviction and RoPE locality to drive prefetch, we enable context lengths that would otherwise exceed GPU memory capacity while maintaining hit rates that preserve inference latency. For industry, as CXL-fabric convergence matures through efforts like Enfabrica and the UEC consortium, this work provides the missing software architecture that makes disaggregated memory genuinely useful for LLM workloads.

Abstract:With the growing demand for long-context LLMs across a wide range of applications, the key-value (KV) cache has become a critical bottleneck for both latency and memory usage. Recently, KV-cache offloading has emerged as a promising approach to reduce memory footprint and inference latency while preserving accuracy. Prior evaluations have largely focused on tasks that do not require extracting large amounts of information from the context. In this work, we study KV-cache offloading on context-intensive tasks: problems where the solution requires looking up a lot of information from the input prompt. We create and release the Text2JSON benchmark, a highly context-intensive task that requires extracting structured knowledge from raw text. We evaluate modern KV offloading on Text2JSON and other context-intensive tasks and find significant performance degradation on both Llama 3 and Qwen 3 models. Our analysis identifies two key reasons for poor accuracy: low-rank projection of keys and unreliable landmarks, and proposes a simpler alternative strategy that significantly improves accuracy across multiple LLM families and benchmarks. evidence.full: Title: KV Cache Offloading for Context-Intensive Tasks # KV Cache Offloading for Context-Intensive Tasks. With the growing demand for long-context LLMs across a wide range of applications, the key–value (KV) cache has become a critical bottleneck for both latency and memory usage. Recently, KV-cache offloading has emerged as a promising approach to reduce memory footprint and inference latency while preserving accuracy. Most recent works on KV offloading evaluate on tasks that do not require extracting large amounts of information from the context. In this work, we study KV-cache offloading on context-intensive tasks: problems where the solution requires looking up a lot of information from the input prompt. We create and release the Text2JSON benchmark, a highly context-intensive task that requires extracting structured knowledge from raw text. We evaluate modern KV offloading on Text2JSON and other context-intensive tasks and find significant performance degradation on both Llama 3 and Qwen3 models. Our analysis identifies two key reasons for poor accuracy: low-rank projection of keys and unreliable selection, and proposes a simpler alternative strategy that significantly improves accuracy across multiple LLM families and benchmarks. These findings highlight the need for a comprehensive and rigorous evaluation of long-context compression techniques. For sufficiently long sequences, the KV cache can require more memory than the model parameters themselves (29). A promising alternative to pruning is KV-cache offloading (3; 71): instead of removing KV entries permanently, these techniques move the original entries to cheaper system memory and load them back when necessary. To avoid loading the full KV cache, they use method-specific heuristics to predict which KV entries will be used at every inference step 39; 14; 76; 78; 91, reporting little to no performance degradation compared to full attention. We systematically evaluate KV offloading methods on context-intensive tasks and observe significant accuracy drops. We identify context-intensive subtasks in existing benchmarks and create a new Text2JSON dataset to evaluate KV offloading on real-world context-intensive tasks without confounding factors. We evaluate several modern KV offloading methods across two LLM families (Llama and Qwen3) and find consistent accuracy drops on context-intensive problems. We analyze the failure modes of KV offloading and find that the accuracy loss is caused by key selection strategies, not KV offloading in principle.

evidence.full: Multi-tier KV Cache and Prefetching. The large memory footprint of KV caches has motivated work on memory tiering and cache reuse for LLM inference. General inference systems such as FlexGen(Sheng et al., 2023) and DeepSpeed Inference(Aminabadi et al., 2022) improve throughput by partitioning model data and intermediate states across GPU, CPU, and NVMe storage, while LLM in a Flash(Alizadeh et al., 2023) and PowerInfer(Song et al., 2023) further explore flash-based offloading for memory-constrained inference. For KV-cache management, PagedAttention(Kwon et al., 2023), Pensieve(Yu et al., 2023), and CachedAttention(Gao et al., 2024) improve paging, placement, and context reuse, while LMCache(Cheng et al., 2025) and Mooncake(Qin et al., 2025) reduce recomputation through KV sharing and [...] LLM serving is becoming increasingly memory-dominated. evidence.full: Storing KV cache in GPU memory for LLM inference can quickly lead to memory saturation, limiting serving scalability and performance. KV cache storage on CPU memory becomes limited as model size and request context length increase. To that extent, we explore CXL memory for KV cache offloading, in which CXL offers expanded capacity with low-latency access. Our preliminary results show that CXL-CPU data transfer has similar latency and bandwidth as the CPU-GPU counterpart. In addition, CXL-based KV cache offloading provides similar performance compared to full KV re-compute on GPUs, while supporting larger workloads. Specifically, using CXL memory for KV cache storage increased the maximum batch size by 30%, while maintaining the same SLO on TTFT. Our cost-efficiency analysis further shows [...] Large language model (LLM) serving systems often store key-value (KV) cache to reduce redundant inference computations. However, storing KV cache of long-context requests under high-throughput serving demand can overwhelm GPU and host memory. Recently, Compute Express Link (CXL) emerges as a promising interconnect technology that offers low-latency host-device communication and expanded memory capacity. In this paper, we explore leveraging CXL memory to store KV cache in LLM serving. Our results show that CXL-CPU interconnect performs comparably to CPU-GPU interconnect in both data-transfer latency and bandwidth, enabling a 30% increase in batch size compared to full KV re-compute under the same SLO. Our production Return on Investment (ROI) modeling further shows that storing KV cache on [...] service-level objective (SLO) for TTFT is typically 400ms . To meet such SLO, LLM serving systems often cache the previously-computed KV data of the preceding tokens (i.e., prefix) in GPU memory, to avoid re-computing them for future requests that have the same prefix [5, 3, 6]. Storing KV cache reduces the overall computational load and significantly improves throughput by trading memory for computation. In production chatbot applications that support large context windows, the demand for KV cache storage grows rapidly by the number of inference requests from users, which cannot be fully accom-modated by the limited and expensive GPU memory . Researchers thus developed techniques to offload KV cache to CPU memory, leveraging the larger CPU memory capacity to reduce GPU memory pressure

evidence.full: Long-context LLM serving is increasingly limited by KV cache movement, not only by GPU compute. As context length and concurrency grow, KV cache exceeds GPU memory and must be spilled, refilled, prefetched, and reused across the memory hierarchy. This is especially challenging for edge AI servers with 4 to 8 GPUs, where host DRAM capacity, DRAM bandwidth, PCIe bandwidth, power, and cost are tightly constrained. A conventional KV offloading path often uses host DRAM as a staging buffer between GPUs and SSDs. At 4-GPU scale, long-context serving can generate roughly 200 GB/s of KV store and refill traffic. If this traffic must enter and leave host DRAM, the staging path can consume roughly 400 GB/s of DRAM bandwidth, making host DRAM both a capacity requirement and a bandwidth bottleneck.

While quantization (Frantar et al., 2022; Lin et al., 2024a) and parameter offloading (Alizadeh et al., 2023; Xue et al., 2024) reduce model footprint, a critical bottleneck lies in managing the key-value (KV) cache. Unlike fixed model weights, the KV cache grows linearly with sequence length and batch size, often surpassing model size (as shown in Fig. 1). On a 4B-parameter LM, batched inputs over 16K tokens already push the KV cache beyond device memory, causing latency spikes or out-of-memory failures. As LMs are increasingly applied to long-context tasks, practical on-device inference requires efficient KV cache [...] On embedded and mobile systems with limited memory capacity (e.g., 8 GiB) and strict per-application quotas (to avoid disrupting other applications and OS services), retaining the full KV cache in memory becomes infeasible. This results in a KV cache memory capacity wall, where the KV cache overtakes model weights as the dominant memory consumer, limiting the scalability of long-context on-device inference. ### 2.3. KV Cache Disk Offloading [...] The design of KVSwap needs to overcome two major challenges introduced by on-device disk offloading. First, the ever-increasing KV-cache size introduced by long-context is a challenge for resource-constrained mobile and embedded devices. The limited memory capacity and strict per-application memory quotas result in a tight memory budget, far beyond what existing KV-cache offloading methods, which were primarily designed for server-side deployments, can accommodate. To address this, KVSwap proposes a compression and reconstruction algorithm that enables aggressive memory compression while still achieving information recovery with adequate quality.

evidence.full: Long-context LLM serving is increasingly limited by KV cache movement, not only by GPU compute. As context length and concurrency grow, KV cache exceeds GPU memory and must be spilled, refilled, prefetched, and reused across the memory hierarchy. This is especially challenging for edge AI servers with 4 to 8 GPUs, where host DRAM capacity, DRAM bandwidth, PCIe bandwidth, power, and cost are tightly constrained. A conventional KV offloading path often uses host DRAM as a staging buffer between GPUs and SSDs. At 4-GPU scale, long-context serving can generate roughly 200 GB/s of KV store and refill traffic. If this traffic must enter and leave host DRAM, the staging path can consume roughly 400 GB/s of DRAM bandwidth, making host DRAM both a capacity requirement and a bandwidth bottleneck.

report_md:
# SUMMARY

이 보고서는 장문맥 멀티턴 에이전트 서비스 도메인에서의 KV 캐시 병목을 완화하는 두 기술, MLA(Multi-head Latent Attention)와 ITME(Inter-Tier Memory Expansion)를 비교한다. 시장성 관점과 도메인 적용 관점에서 각각의 장단점이 다르게 드러난다. MLA는 소프트웨어적 접근으로 주요 추론 스택과 일부 모델에 통합되어 도입이 상대적으로 용이하나, 생태계 확장성과 제3자 검증, 직접적 시장성 수치가 부족하다. ITME는 하드웨어-소프트웨어 협력 기반으로 대용량 메모리 확장과 지연 마스킹을 실험적으로 보였으나, 상용화·생태계 확장 근거와 정확도 평가가 부족하다. 두 기술 모두 도입 전제와 운영 복잡도, 외부 검증의 부족 등에서 관점에 따라 평가가 엇갈린다. 도메인 전환 시, MLA는 온디바이스 환경에서 인프라 요구가 장애가 되고, ITME는 클라우드 환경에서는 확장성 가능성이 있으나 온디바이스에서는 적용 자체가 어렵다.

## 1. 분석 배경

장문맥 멀티턴 에이전트 서비스는 단일 세션에서 100K 토큰이 넘는 문맥을 유지하며, 대화가 이어질수록 KV 캐시가 턴마다 누적된다. 이때 메모리 용량과 대역폭이 병목이 되며, 특히 대규모 LLM에서는 KV 캐시가 수백 GB에 달해 동시 세션 처리와 비용 효율성에 큰 영향을 준다. MLA와 ITME는 이 병목을 각각 소프트웨어적 압축과 하드웨어-소프트웨어 협력 기반 오프로드로 접근한다. MLA는 Transformer 내에서 KV 캐시를 저차원 잠재 벡터로 압축해 메모리 사용량을 줄이고, ITME는 CXL 하이브리드 메모리 계층에 KV 캐시와 모델 가중치를 오프로드해 용량 병목을 완화한다. 두 접근은 요구 인프라, 도입 난이도, 운영 복잡도, 생태계 확장성 등에서 차이가 크며, 시장성 및 실제 워크로드 적용 가능성에 따라 평가가 달라진다.

## 2. 기술 선정

본 비교는 MLA와 ITME 두 기술을 선정해 진행했다. 선정 기준은 장문맥 멀티턴 에이전트 서비스에서의 KV 캐시 병목 완화에 초점을 두고, 소프트웨어적 접근과 하드웨어-소프트웨어 협력 접근을 대표하는 기술을 각각 고르는 것이었다. 후보군은 공개 논문, 기술 보고서, 주요 추론 스택의 통합 사례, 시장 전망 보고서 등에서 직접 수집했다. 최종 선정은 사람이 직접 근거를 검토해 결정했다.

## 3. 기술 개요

### MLA

MLA(Multi-head Latent Attention)는 Transformer 프레임워크 내에서 KV 캐시를 저차원 잠재 벡터로 압축하는 방식이다. MHA(Multi-head Attention) 대비 동일 또는 더 나은 성능을 유지하면서 KV 캐시 요구량을 크게 줄인다. DeepSeek 67B 모델 기준, KV 캐시를 93.3% 줄이고, 최대 생성 처리량을 5.76배 높이며, 학습 비용을 42.5% 절감했다고 보고되었다. MLA는 대규모 MoE 언어모델과 128K 이상의 장문맥을 지원하는 환경에서 동작하며, 모델이 MHA와 저차원 KV 압축을 지원해야 한다. 저자가 밝힌 한계는 근거에 없다.

### ITME

ITME(Inter-Tier Memory Expansion)는 LLM의 대용량 KV 캐시와 모델 가중치를 CXL 하이브리드 메모리 기반 원격 확장 계층에 오프로드한다. 하드웨어/소프트웨어 선행 로딩과 PCIe Gen5 인터페이스를 통해 지연과 네트워크 오버헤드를 숨긴다. CPU-offload 베이스라인(128GB 호스트 메모리) 대비 최대 35.7% 처리량 개선을 보고했다[ITME p.10]. ITME는 고속 GPU/호스트 메모리, CXL 하이브리드 메모리, PCIe Gen5, NVMe SSD 등 멀티티어 메모리 계층이 필요하다. 성능 변동(경합 시 I/O stall)과 PCIe Gen4 시스템의 대역폭 한계가 언급되었으나, PCIe Gen5로 일부 해소했다[ITME p.11].

## 4. 관점별 평가

### 4.1 시장성 관점

## 5. 시사점

관점에 따라 동일한 근거가 다르게 해석된다. MLA는 시장성 관점에서는 주요 추론 스택 통합과 낮은 진입 비용이 강조되지만, 도메인 적용 관점에서는 특수 커널과 추가 연산으로 인한 운영 복잡도가 부각된다. ITME는 시장성에서는 신규 하드웨어 도입 필요성이 진입 비용으로, 도메인에서는 실제 상용 환경에서의 적용 가능성(프로토타입 한계)이 더 중요한 이슈로 다뤄진다. 두 기술 모두 외부 검증 부족이 시장성에서는 확산성 한계, 도메인에서는 실증 신뢰성 부족으로 다르게 읽힌다.

도메인 전환 시 평가가 크게 달라진다. MLA는 온디바이스 추론 환경에서는 대규모 모델과 인프라 요구로 인해 적용이 어렵고, ITME는 CXL 하이브리드 메모리 기반 아키텍처가 온디바이스 환경에 적용 불가해 사실상 도입이 불가능하다. 반면 클라우드 대규모 동시 서빙 환경에서는 MLA의 KV 캐시 절감 효과와 주요 추론 스택 통합이 유리하게 작용할 수 있고, ITME도 대용량 메모리 확장으로 확장성 가능성을 보이나, 실제 상용 환경 검증이 부족하다. 즉, 두 기술 모두 도메인 전환 시 막히는 지점이 다르며, 같은 조건에서 똑같이 불리해지는 것이 아니라 각기 다른 한계에 부딪힌다.

## 6. 한계점

이 평가는 공개 정보 기반으로 진행되었으며, 반도체 업계의 실제 채택 규모나 원가, 수율 등은 확인할 수 없다. 기술 성숙도(TRL)와 이해관계자 관점은 범위에서 제외했다. 확증편향을 막기 위해 두 기술에 동일한 질문 템플릿을 적용하고, 유리·불리 근거를 각각 따로 수집했으며, 기술 제시 순서를 바꿔도 결론이 달라지지 않는지 확인했다. 모든 평가 문장에는 근거 원장의 id를 달았다. 웹 근거 중 일부는 개별 기술이 아니라 LLM 비용 최적화, CXL 메모리 확장 등 상위 범주에 대한 것이었으며, 해당 항목은 기술 고유 근거로 사용하지 않았다. 근거가 없는 항목은 "근거 없음"으로 명시했다. 이 조치들은 관점별 대칭성과 근거의 직접성을 높이기 위한 것이나, 실제 시장 채택 현황, 상용화 수준, 장기적 신뢰성 등은 여전히 불확실하다.
